generation.hypothesis: The degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by the formation of nanoscale deformation twins and the migration of dislocations, which can lead to catastrophic failure due to the accumulation of internal stresses and the formation of high-energy sites.

cited_evidence.text: This study systematically investigates the role of Mo additions in FeCoCrNi and Fe0.5CoCrNi alloys fabricated via L-PBF. Alloys with varying Mo contents (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15) were evaluated in terms of microstructure, mechanical performance, and electrochemical behavior in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and 60 °C. The results demonstrate that while all alloys exhibit good corrosion resistance at room temperature, Mo-free alloys suffer severe degradation at elevated temperature. In contrast, Fe0.5CoCrNiMo0.1 combines the highest strength with superior corrosion resistance, owing to Mo-induced optimization of the passive film structure and enhanced Cr2O3 formation. These findings provide fundamental insights into Mo-doping mechanisms and establish design guidelines for engineering FeCoCrNi-based HEAs in aggressive environments.

In this report, we establish a force-field for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy and validate it by comparing structural properties, relative stability, and pair probabilities with first-principles calculations and limited experimental results. After the validation, we employ the new potential to investigate the large-scale deformation characteristics of Al0.1CrCoFeNi using atomistic MD simulations. Thus, we address the absence of well-developed force-field functions for high-entropy alloys and provide the EAM-LJ parameters to define the self- and cross-interactions of the participating elements in the alloy. In Al0.1CrCoFeNi, the electronic-structure-based linear-response calculations predict clustering driven by Al-Ni pair correlations (forcing Al-Al and Ni-Ni clustering behavior). The MD simulations are in agreement with the clustering trend, as given by the large clustering domains of like pairs dominated by Al-Al. Although an increase in temperature reduces the clustering strength of like pairs, Al-Al correlations still dominate. In summary, owing to higher volume fractions and higher APB energy of γ′ precipitates, HESA can show the superior tensile yield strength to those of the reported high entropy alloys from room to elevated temperatures. In addition, the high temperature strength of HESA can approach that of the Ni-based superalloy CMSX-2, and the optimizations in larger γ′ size, higher degree of misfit value may contribute to further strengthening. Regarding to creep resistances, HESA can be strengthened by the lower stacking fault energy, higher creep activation energy and stable γ′ phases; the sluggish diffusion of the high entropy γ matrix may have attributed to the higher creep activation energy. At higher temperature, although the P-raft γ′ at 982 °C has led to a more rapid increase in creep strain rate, the creep life of HESA can be compared to those of some conventional superalloys and with less refractory contents. Therefore, HESA can be a promising new type of high temperature alloy with improved cost-performance. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has been focused on understanding their microstructure, mechanical properties, and degradation mechanisms under various conditions. Earlier studies have investigated the corrosion behavior, thermal stability, and tensile properties of these alloys. Recent studies have employed advanced characterization techniques, such as atomistic simulations and phase-field modeling, to reveal the underlying mechanisms of deformation twinning and stress corrosion cracking. The trend suggests a growing interest in understanding the nanoscale mechanisms governing the behavior of high-entropy alloys.
decision.unsolved: The degradation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases are not fully understood, and the role of intrinsic edge dislocations in promoting high-temperature strength and ductility is still being explored.
decision.lever: atomistic simulations with reactive force fields
decision.why: To investigate the degradation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases, and to reveal the role of intrinsic edge dislocations in promoting high-temperature strength and ductility, atomistic simulations with reactive force fields can be employed. This approach can provide insights into the nanoscale mechanisms governing the behavior of high-entropy alloys and help design new alloys with improved properties.
